information.content: Broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antimicrobial with good tissue, ocular and CNS penetration. In exotics it is reserved for specific indications such as resistant infections or deep ocular/CNS disease.
Human exposure carries serious safety concerns. Use gloves and restrict to individual animals where there is a clear indication.
Topical antiseptic used for skin, wound and surgical-site preparation. It is not consistently effective as a sole antifungal.
Do not use in eyes, do not instil into ears if tympanic integrity is unknown, and avoid use in amphibians.
Topical non-selective beta-blocker used for glaucoma by reducing aqueous humour production.
Systemic absorption can cause bradycardia and hypotension. Avoid in uncontrolled heart failure and asthma.
Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used to reduce aqueous humour production in glaucoma and ocular hypertension.
Dorzolamide/timolol combinations may cause miosis and are not ideal for uveitis or anterior lens luxation.
Fourth-generation topical fluoroquinolone for selected bacterial ocular infections, including some Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens.
Reserve ophthalmic fluoroquinolones for appropriate infections where narrower options are unsuitable or ineffective.
Topical fluoroquinolone used when other ocular antibacterial agents are unsuitable or ineffective. It has useful corneal penetration.
Reserve for appropriate ocular infections and reassess if response is poor.
Aminoglycoside antibiotic for culture-supported Gram-negative infections and selected topical/nebulised indications. It is concentration-dependent and potentially nephrotoxic.
Ensure hydration and renal function. Avoid concurrent nephrotoxic, ototoxic or neuromuscular-blocking drugs where possible.
Aminoglycoside antibiotic with particular usefulness against Pseudomonas in selected avian and reptile cases.
Monitor renal function and hydration; give IV slowly if used intravenously.
Topical antimicrobial/antifungal cream used for burns, flystrike, wounds and selected external bacterial infections, including fish wounds.
Use gloves. Avoid in neonates or pregnant animals and consider hepatic/renal accumulation if large areas are treated.
Topical imidazole antifungal for dermatophyte, Malassezia, Candida-associated skin/ear disease and selected amphibian mycoses.
Avoid steroid-containing preparations when steroid exposure is undesirable, especially in rabbits, birds and pregnant animals.
Polyene antifungal used mainly for Candida/GI yeast overgrowth and selected topical mycoses. It is not absorbed from the GI tract.
Oral IU/kg rows are not mg/kg calculator rows and should stay out of the standard mg/kg dose calculator.
Triazole antifungal used for aspergillosis, fungal keratitis, dermatomycoses and selected amphibian chytridiomycosis protocols.
Avoid in pregnancy and liver disease. Macaws, some raptors and some snake species may be particularly sensitive.

warnings.warning_text: Reserve for specific cases because of resistance and human safety concerns.
Can cause dose-related bone marrow suppression and has important hepatic enzyme interactions.
Mucosal and skin irritation can occur, especially with stronger or inappropriate preparations.
Do not use in eyes and avoid amphibian skin exposure.
Can cause miosis, conjunctival hyperaemia and local irritation.
Systemic absorption may cause bradycardia and reduced blood pressure.
Local irritation and blepharitis may occur.
Avoid or use caution with severe hepatic or renal impairment.
Local ocular irritation may occur after application.
Fluoroquinolone stewardship still applies, even for topical therapy.
Local irritation and ocular discomfort may occur.
Fluoroquinolone stewardship applies to ophthalmic use.
Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are clinically important risks.
Avoid in dehydration or renal compromise unless benefits clearly outweigh risk.
Aminoglycoside toxicity includes renal, otic and neuromuscular effects.
Do not use ophthalmic product where corneal ulceration is present.
Sulphonamide-sensitive patients may react and systemic absorption can occur over large wounds.
Avoid in neonates and pregnant animals.
Topical preparations vary and some combinations contain corticosteroids or antibiotics.
Do not treat dermatophytosis as a dab-and-dash problem; continue appropriate environmental and duration control.
Efficacy varies by indication; macrorhabdiasis response is uncertain.
Avoid steroid-containing topical combinations when steroid exposure is inappropriate.
Hepatic and GI adverse effects can occur and some avian/reptile species are sensitive.
Do not use in cottonmouth snakes or Dumeril’s ground boas.

pearls.pearl: Chloramphenicol is a useful locked cupboard drug, not a sweet jar antimicrobial.
Chlorhexidine is a cleaner, not a magic antifungal cloak. Dilution is the spellbook.
A tiny eye drop can still behave like a beta-blocker. Respect the drop dragon.
Dorzolamide lowers pressure, but angry eyes still need diagnosis, not just more drops.
Topical fluoroquinolones are not eye glitter. Use them when the bug deserves them.
Ofloxacin gets into cornea nicely, but culture still outranks guesswork when things go swampy.
Gentamicin is a sharp tool. Hydration is the handle.
Tobramycin may be kinder than gentamicin, but it is still carrying aminoglycoside teeth.
Silver sulfadiazine is wound armour, not wallpaper. Thin, targeted use wins.
Miconazole works best when the environment stops re-seeding the fungus confetti cannon.
Nystatin stays mostly in the gut, which is either exactly the point or entirely not the point.
Voriconazole is the fancy antifungal scalpel. Excellent in the right claws, nasty in the wrong snake.
